# Typst

For Typst the extension prints each index with page locators, in two columns,
built from the same marks every other back-end reads. A declared index that no
mark files in prints nothing, not even its heading. It needs no Typst
package: everything the index uses is written into the document, so nothing is
downloaded when the document compiles.

A page number is known only once Typst has laid out the pages, and the
extension runs before that. So it writes an invisible Typst label at each mark,
and each locator in the index asks Typst for the page of its label while the
document is typeset. A mark in a heading gets its label just after the
heading, so the copy of that heading in the table of contents carries none.
For the same reason, a mark in the caption of most figures, tables and code
listings gets its label in the float's content. See [Lists of figures, tables
and listings](#lists-of-figures-tables-and-listings) for which floats.

## Where the index goes

Each index goes where your placement marker puts it, and at the end of the
document where no marker names it, in the order your `indexes:` metadata
declares them. See [Placing the index](placing-the-index.qmd). An index starts
on a new page under an unnumbered level-one heading, which Typst lists in the
table of contents. The heading is the title your `indexes:` metadata gives the
index, or its name where you give no title. A document that declares no
`indexes:` gets **Index**, or its language's word for an index where the
extension covers that language. The text after the index starts on a new page
too.

## Entries

The entries are ordered and grouped as in HTML: a `Symbols` group first, then
one group per letter, each under its letter in bold. See [Letter groups in the
HTML index](letter-groups.qmd). A sub-entry is indented under its parent, and
sub-entries nest as deep as you write them.

## Locators

Each locator is the page number as the page shows it. Each one links to its
page.

- Where the page numbering pattern names two counters, such as `1 / 1`,
  a locator prints both, as the page footer does: `5 / 30`.
- A page with no numbering prints its physical page number.
- Several marks of one term on one page print that page once.
- Locators that print the same text print it once, even from different
  pages, as after a page counter reset. That one locator links to the earliest
  of those pages, and it is bold where any of their marks is a principal
  mention. It prints at the place of the first of them in the order below.
- The locator of a principal mention is set in bold. Where a principal and an
  ordinary mark of one term share a page, that page's one locator is bold.
- A range prints its opening and closing pages, `12–15`, and links to the
  opening page. Where both ends of a range are on one page, with no page
  counter update between them, it prints that page alone. Where the two ends print the same text, it prints that text alone.
- An entry's locators are ordered by the numbering of their opening pages, as
  the PDF index orders page numbers. Lower roman numbers come first, then upper
  roman numbers, arabic numbers, lowercase letters, uppercase letters, and then
  any other numbering. The first counting symbol of the page numbering pattern
  sets the kind, so `1 / 1` is arabic. A page with no numbering counts as
  arabic, with its physical page as its number, and a numbering function
  counts as other. Numbers of one kind are ordered by value, the page
  counter's value or the physical page where a page has no numbering, and
  then by page. So after a page counter reset, `1` comes before a `3` from an
  earlier page. Where two locators of one kind and number open on one page,
  the one that closes on the earlier page comes first, and a single mark comes
  before a range that closes on its page.
- A range whose two ends print different numbers of one kind, with a higher
  closing number, spans the numbers from its opening number to its closing
  number, both included. A mark of the term on a spanned number of that kind prints no
  locator of its own, even on a page after the range, as after a page counter
  reset. A principal mention there loses its bold. A range whose two ends
  print the same text counts as a single mark, and a span removes it the same
  way. Any other range spans nothing. A span never removes a range whose two
  ends print different text.
- Pages you marked separately stay separate: marks on pages 3, 4 and 5 print
  `3, 4, 5`. Only a range you write prints as a range. A mark on the page just
  after a range prints its own locator, `2–3, 4`, where the PDF index prints
  `2–4`.

## Cross-references

A cross-reference prints its word in italics, then its target as plain text,
with no link. Two targets of one kind share one word: `see Felines; Pets`. The words are `see` and `see also`, your document language's
words where the extension covers that language, or the words you set under
`index-labels:`, which Typst reads for `symbols`, `see` and `see-also`.

The punctuation is fixed: a comma before each locator and before the first
cross-reference, and a semicolon between two cross-references. The
`separator` and `xref-separator` keys of `index-labels:` do not reach the Typst
index.

## Books

Quarto renders a Typst book as one merged document, so the extension sees every
chapter's marks at once, and a range you open in one chapter and close in
another pairs. Books were tested on Quarto 1.10.18. On that version Quarto's
Typst book template does not compile a book whose `book:` metadata has no
`author:`. Quarto 1.5.52 does not render a Typst book. It prints the warning
`The typst format is not supported by book projects` and writes no PDF.

## Lists of figures, tables and listings

When this page was written, `lof: true` printed no list of figures in a Typst
document (observed on Quarto 1.10.19, 2026-10-19). To print one, write Typst's
own `outline` in a raw Typst block:

````markdown
```{=typst}
#outline(title: [List of Figures], target: figure.where(kind: "quarto-float-fig"))
```
````

A list of tables takes the kind `quarto-float-tbl`, and a list of code listings
takes `quarto-float-lst`. Such a list copies each caption it lists. Take a
figure, a figure div, a table or a code listing whose content is one image or
paragraph, one table or one code block. A mark in its caption gets its label in
that content, so the mark files the page its caption prints on. An id you
give it names one place, so a link to it builds. Both hold when the float does
not break across pages, which is Quarto's default. In a document that makes
floats breakable, such a mark files the page where the float's content ends.

Any other float keeps a caption mark's label in the caption, because moving
it into that content changed the layout. A list before such a float files the
mark on the list's page. An id you give the mark is copied with the caption,
so a Typst link to it fails to compile. These floats include a float laid out
in cells with `layout-ncol` or its kin, such as a grid of images or tables. A
code listing with a `filename` is one, as is a figure or table whose content
Quarto keeps in a code cell's output div, as a knitr `kable` does. They also
include a figure with no id whose content does not start with text or an
image, which Markdown does not make. A knitr plot and a table knitr writes
with `output: asis` take the label in their content.

## A mark Typst never prints

A mark in a front-matter field that Quarto's Typst template does not print,
such as `description:`, has no label on any page, so it adds no page number.
If all the page-number marks of an entry are such marks, and it has no
cross-reference and no sub-entry that prints, the Typst index leaves it out.
A letter group none of whose entries prints has no heading. Such an entry
that is kept for a sub-entry that prints shows no page number of its own, and
so does an entry whose range opens in such a field and closes on a page.

A `see=` or `see-also=` mark in such a field adds no cross-reference. A
cross-reference prints where one of the marks that write it is on a page.
A cross-reference whose target term is left out is not printed, and nothing
reports it. Where the target was the first of its kind, the word `see` or
`see also` goes in front of the next target of that kind that prints. An
entry left with nothing that prints is left out. Two terms whose
cross-references point at each other both print, if a mark of each is on a
page. A target that no mark files still prints, and the dangling-target
report names it. An index whose every entry is left out prints nothing: no
heading, no line in the table of contents and no page, as an index that no
mark files in prints nothing.
